chapters: Per se and quid pro quo
De facto and the status quo

units.t: Latin You Already Speak.
Part one. Bona fide and ad hoc.
You might not think of yourself as a Latin speaker.
But if you've ever talked about the status quo, or said you were a bona fide fan of something, you've been speaking Latin.
It's a language that stopped being anyone's mother tongue well over a thousand years ago.
Latin lived on for centuries in the church, in universities, in medicine and especially in law.
Even today, Australian courts and contracts still use a fair bit of it.
Educated English speakers sprinkled it through their writing, and some of those phrases stuck so firmly that we now use them without a second thought.
Let's look at six of them, what they actually mean, and how to use them naturally.
First, bona fide.
It's two words.
B, O, N, A.
Then F, I, D, E.
Here's an everyday example.
After twenty years of Saturday matches, she's a bona fide expert on junior netball.
Literally, bona fide means in good faith.
Bona is good, and fide comes from fides, meaning faith or trust.
You can hear the same root in the word fidelity, and even in the old dog name Fido, which in Latin means I trust.
In law, a bona fide purchaser is someone who bought something honestly, without knowing there was a problem with it.
In everyday speech, the meaning has shifted a little.
Bona fide now mostly means genuine, real, the actual thing.
A bona fide offer is a real one, not a bluff.
A bona fide Aussie legend is someone who has earned the title.
You'll hear it pronounced a few ways.
Many Australians say bone-a fide, rhyming with side.
Others say bone-a fie-dee.
Both are widely accepted, so don't let anyone tell you off.
Our second phrase is ad hoc.
A, D.
Then H, O, C.
For example, we formed an ad hoc committee to sort out the Christmas party.
Ad hoc means for this, as in, for this particular purpose.
An ad hoc arrangement is set up to deal with one situation, rather than being part of a permanent plan.
If your workplace has a proper roster, that's a system.
If three people sort out who's covering Friday in the car park, that's ad hoc.
Here's the subtle bit.
Ad hoc isn't automatically a criticism.
Sometimes a quick, one-off solution is exactly right.
But when someone says a company's safety checks were done on an ad hoc basis, they usually mean there was no proper system at all, and that's a problem.
Part two. Per se and quid pro quo.
Our third phrase is per se.
P, E, R.
Then S, E.
For example, I don't hate camping per se, I just hate sleeping on the ground.
Per se means by itself, or in itself.
You use it to separate the thing itself from something connected to it.
In the camping example, the camping isn't the problem.
The hard ground is.
That's the real job of per se.
It says, I'm talking about this exact thing, not all the stuff that comes with it.
Here's another example.
The new phone isn't expensive per se, but the plan you need to go with it certainly is.
One common mistake is writing it as per say.
It's easy to see why, since that's exactly how it sounds.
But it's Latin per, meaning by, and se, meaning itself.
Our fourth phrase is quid pro quo.
Q, U, I, D.
Then P, R, O.
Then Q, U, O.
For example, I'll help you move house on Saturday, but it's a quid pro quo, you're helping me paint the fence.
Quid pro quo means something for something.
It's a fair exchange, one favour in return for another.
Here's a surprising detail from its history.
In the 1500s, the phrase was used by apothecaries, the chemists of the day.
A quid pro quo was when one medicine was swapped for another.
Sometimes that was deliberate, because the proper ingredient was unavailable.
Sometimes it was a mistake, which could be dangerous.
Over time, the phrase moved away from medicine and came to mean any exchange of one thing for another.
Today, it can be perfectly innocent, like our house move and our fence.
But in news reports, quid pro quo often carries a shady tone.
When a journalist asks whether there was a quid pro quo between a donor and a politician, they're asking whether a favour was bought.
So it's worth being a little careful where you use it.
Part three. De facto and the status quo.
Our fifth phrase is one Australians hear more than most.
De facto.
D, E.
Then F, A, C, T, O.
For example, Sam never applied for the job, but he's become the de facto leader of the team.
De facto means in fact, or in practice.
Its partner phrase is de jure, which means by law.
The difference is really useful.
Something is de jure when it's official on paper.
Something is de facto when it's simply how things actually work.
Plenty of countries have a de jure capital city and a de facto one.
Bolivia is a good example.
Its constitution names Sucre as the capital, but the government actually sits in La Paz.
So Sucre is the capital by law, and La Paz is the capital in practice.
In a workplace, the manager might be the de jure boss, while the person everyone actually asks is the de facto boss.
In Australia, of course, de facto has a second, very everyday meaning.
A de facto partner is someone you live with as a couple without being married.
Many Australian laws and government services recognise de facto relationships.
The rules about what counts can be quite detailed, so if it matters for your situation, check the official sources, like the ATO or Services Australia.
Our sixth and final phrase is status quo.
S, T, A, T, U, S.
Then Q, U, O.
For example, the council decided to keep the status quo and leave the car park exactly as it is.
Status quo means the existing state of affairs, the way things currently are.
It's short for a longer Latin phrase, status quo ante, meaning the state in which things were before.
Diplomats used a version of it to describe peace deals that put everything back as it had been before a war.
Today, you'll often hear about people who want to challenge the status quo, or defend it.
Businesses talk about disrupting the status quo.
Older hands at work sometimes defend it, on the grounds that the current way has worked for years.
Psychologists even have a name for our tendency to stick with things as they are, simply because change feels like effort.
They call it status quo bias.
It's one reason so many people stay on the same phone plan or electricity deal for years, even when a better one is available.
The phrase is useful precisely because it's neutral.
It describes how things are, without saying whether that's good or bad.
So how do you use Latin like this without sounding stuffy?
Here are three quick tips.
First, only use the Latin when it's the shortest, clearest option.
Per se is handy because the English alternative takes more words.
But saying inter alia instead of among other things just makes you sound like a court document.
Second, get the meaning exactly right.
Ad hoc doesn't mean random, and bona fide doesn't mean very.
Used precisely, these phrases sound confident.
Used loosely, they sound like showing off.
Third, say them plainly.
There's no need for a special accent or a pause for effect.
Say de facto the way you'd say any other word, and it'll sound completely natural.
To sum up, bona fide means genuine, ad hoc means for one purpose, and per se means in itself.
Quid pro quo is an exchange, de facto means in practice, and status quo is the way things are now.
Use them when they're the neatest way to say what you mean, and you'll sound clear rather than clever.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does bona fide literally mean?
Answer. In good faith. Today it usually means genuine.
Question two. What's the difference between de facto and de jure?
Answer. De facto means in fact or in practice. De jure means by law.
Question three. What did quid pro quo originally describe in the 1500s?
Answer. Swapping one medicine for another, sometimes by mistake.
That's the end of Latin You Already Speak. Nicely done.
